The paper presents an algorithm for computing Hecke eigensystems associated with Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms. These eigensystems encode the action of Hecke operators on spaces of automorphic forms and are central to understanding the arithmetic and representation-theoretic properties of the forms in question. By developing an explicit computational method, the paper provides a practical tool for investigating examples that would otherwise be difficult to access.

The algorithm is designed for Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms defined over real quadratic fields with narrow class number one. This setting is particularly suitable for explicit computation, since the assumption on the narrow class number simplifies the arithmetic of ideals and allows the relevant modular and Hecke-theoretic structures to be handled more effectively. The method therefore contributes to the computational study of automorphic forms beyond the classical case over \(\mathbb{Q}\).

To illustrate the algorithm, the paper includes examples over the real quadratic field \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})\). These examples demonstrate how the method can be applied in practice and show how Hecke eigenvalues can be computed for concrete spaces of Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms. The field \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})\) serves as a natural test case because it is one of the simplest real quadratic fields and has narrow class number one.

In these computations, the authors identify Hilbert-Siegel eigenforms whose Hecke eigensystems suggest that they may arise as lifts from Hilbert eigenforms. Such lifts are important because they connect different types of automorphic forms and provide evidence for broader functorial relationships predicted by the Langlands program. The examples therefore not only illustrate the effectiveness of the algorithm but also point toward interesting arithmetic phenomena that merit further investigation.

outputs.L5:
Hecke, Hilbert, and Siegel are three names that mark central directions in modern number theory, especially in the theory of modular forms and automorphic forms.

Erich Hecke developed many of the foundational ideas surrounding modular forms and L-functions. His work introduced what are now called Hecke operators, algebraic operators acting on spaces of modular forms. These operators reveal deep arithmetic structure: their eigenvalues often encode important number-theoretic information, such as Fourier coefficients of modular forms and data related to elliptic curves and Galois representations.

David Hilbert’s influence appears in several related areas, most notably through Hilbert modular forms. These are generalizations of classical modular forms from the rational numbers to totally real number fields. Instead of studying functions on the complex upper half-plane alone, Hilbert modular forms live on products of upper half-planes, one for each real embedding of the number field. They provide a natural setting for exploring arithmetic over number fields and play an important role in the Langlands program.

Carl Ludwig Siegel contributed another major generalization: Siegel modular forms. These extend classical modular forms to higher-dimensional analogues of the upper half-plane, now called Siegel upper half-spaces. Siegel modular forms are closely connected with abelian varieties, quadratic forms, theta functions, and symplectic groups. They are fundamental in the study of moduli spaces of principally polarized abelian varieties.

Together, the terms Hecke, Hilbert, and Siegel point toward a broad landscape where algebra, analysis, geometry, and arithmetic meet. Hecke operators provide the structural tools, Hilbert modular forms extend modularity to totally real fields, and Siegel modular forms open the theory to higher-dimensional geometric objects. Their interaction continues to shape research in arithmetic geometry, automorphic representations, and the Langlands program.

We present algorithms and computations for Hilbert–Siegel modular forms over real quadratic fields of narrow class number one. Building on the theory of adelic Hilbert–Siegel modular forms and their Fourier expansions, we describe an explicit framework for representing forms, enumerating Fourier coefficients, and performing arithmetic operations in spaces of prescribed weight and level. Particular attention is given to the genus two case, where the Fourier coefficients are indexed by totally positive semi-definite symmetric matrices over the inverse different.

We develop methods for computing Hecke operators, constructing Eisenstein series and cusp forms, and determining bases of spaces of Hilbert–Siegel modular forms. The assumption on the narrow class number ensures a simplified description of cusps and allows the use of global coordinates, making the computational approach more explicit. We also discuss implementation details, including reduction theory over real quadratic fields and precision management for truncated Fourier expansions.

As applications, we compute examples over several real quadratic fields, compare the resulting Hecke eigenvalues with predicted arithmetic data, and illustrate congruences and dimension phenomena in low weights. These computations provide evidence for expected generalizations of classical results on Siegel modular forms and offer a foundation for further exploration of automorphic forms and associated Galois representations over totally real fields.
